Since he is hosting a dinner, he was presumably no longer afflicted, though the text does not say."},{"verse":3,"phrase":"pure nard","lemma":"πιστικός","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"pure nard; spikenard","note":"The adjective describing the nard is rare and its meaning is uncertain. Nard was an aromatic oil imported from the East, which explains its price."},{"verse":5,"phrase":"three hundred denarii","lemma":"δηνάριον","kind":"background","traditional":"three hundred pence; three hundred denarii","note":"A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a laborer. Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year’s wages."},{"verse":9,"phrase":"good news","lemma":"εὐαγγέλιον","kind":"departure","traditional":"gospel","note":"The Greek word was an ordinary term for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”"},{"verse":10,"phrase":"hand him over","lemma":"παραδίδωμι","kind":"departure","traditional":"betray him","note":"Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same word for what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate and what Pilate then does. “Betray” names the treachery the context supplies, and some scholars defend it as a legitimate contextual sense; “hand over” lets the reader see the repeated word, as in verses 11, 18, 21, 41, 42 and 44."},{"verse":27,"phrase":"fall away","lemma":"σκανδαλίζω","kind":"departure","traditional":"be offended","note":"The older rendering “be offended” now suggests hurt feelings. The verb pictures being tripped up so as to fall from loyalty, and here it refers to the disciples’ desertion that night; most modern versions also say “fall away.” The quotation that follows is from Zechariah 13:7."},{"verse":36,"phrase":"Abba, Father","lemma":"ἀββά","kind":"background","traditional":"Abba, Father","note":"Abba is the Aramaic word for “father,” used in addressing one’s own father by children and adults alike. Mark preserves the Aramaic and adds the Greek equivalent. The once-popular claim that it is baby talk equivalent to “Daddy” is no longer widely held."},{"verse":38,"phrase":"testing","lemma":"πειρασμός","kind":"departure","traditional":"temptation","note":"Most versions have “temptation” here; some have “the time of trial.” In the usage of the period the word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will remain faithful, which is what the disciples are about to face. English “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin. Lexicons recognize both senses, and the two overlap here."},{"verse":41,"phrase":"Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough!","lemma":"ἀπέχω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"Sleep on now, and take your rest: it is enough","note":"The first sentence can be read as a question, as a command (“Sleep on now and rest”), or as a reproachful exclamation. The single Greek word rendered “Enough!” is among the most debated in Mark: its usual meanings were “he has received in full” or “it is distant,” and proposals include “It is settled” and “He has been paid,” referring to Judas. “Enough” is the most common rendering but is uncertain."},{"verse":47,"phrase":"slave","lemma":"δοῦλος","kind":"departure","traditional":"servant","note":"The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. Some modern versions also say “slave.” The same applies to the “slave girls” of verses 66 and 69, where the Greek word means a female slave and is traditionally rendered “maid” or “servant girl.”"},{"verse":48,"phrase":"bandit","lemma":"λῃστής","kind":"departure","traditional":"robber; thief","note":"The Greek word denotes an armed, violent plunderer such as a highwayman, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some versions render it “rebel” here; that reading is possible but not certain. Most modern versions have “robber.”"},{"verse":58,"phrase":"sanctuary","lemma":"ναός","kind":"departure","traditional":"temple","note":"Greek has two words usually both rendered “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts (as in verse 49) and this one for the building in which God was held to dwell. “Sanctuary” keeps them distinct. Most versions use “temple” for both, and scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers observe the distinction."},{"verse":61,"phrase":"Messiah","lemma":"Χριστός","kind":"departure","traditional":"Christ","note":"The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one,” the king Israel expected. Here it is a title under examination, not a name, so “Messiah” is used; several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. “Christ” is kept where the word functions as part of Jesus’ name."},{"verse":62,"phrase":"the Power","lemma":"δύναμις","kind":"background","traditional":"power","note":"“The Power,” like “the Blessed One” in the high priest’s question, is a reverent way of referring to God without naming him. Jesus’ reply combines Psalm 110:1, where the king sits at God’s right hand, with Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven."},{"verse":68,"phrase":"and a rooster crowed","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"and the cock crew","note":"These words are missing from several important early manuscripts, and some critical editions bracket them. They may have been added to prepare for the “second time” of verse 72, or removed to match the other Gospels, which mention only one crowing. The Greek text followed here includes them."},{"verse":70,"phrase":"and your speech is like theirs","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"and thy speech agreeth thereto","note":"These words are absent from the earliest manuscripts and from most modern translations, though they stand in the majority of later manuscripts and in the King James Version. Many scholars think they were added under the influence of Matthew 26:73. The Greek text followed here includes them."},{"verse":71,"phrase":"call down curses","lemma":"ἀναθεματίζω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"to curse and to swear","note":"The verb means to place someone under a curse, and no object is expressed. Most understand that Peter invoked a curse on himself if he was lying; some scholars think he cursed Jesus. The traditional “curse and swear” can wrongly suggest profanity, whereas the Greek describes a solemn curse and a sworn denial."},{"verse":72,"phrase":"he broke down and wept","lemma":"ἐπιβάλλω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"when he thought thereon, he wept","note":"The Greek participle before “wept” is obscure. Proposals include “he broke down,” “he began to,” “when he thought about it,” “he rushed outside,” and “covering his head.” None has won general agreement."}],"candidates":[{"lemma":"δοῦλος","rendering":"slave","verse":47,"reason":"Recurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between “servant” and “slave,” which changes how readers picture households, parables and Paul’s self-descriptions."},{"lemma":"συνέδριον","rendering":"council","verse":55,"reason":"Versions vary between “council” and the loanword “Sanhedrin” across the Gospels and Acts, and the choice should be uniform."},{"lemma":"γρηγορέω","rendering":"keep awake","verse":34,"reason":"Rendered variously “watch,” “keep watch,” “stay awake” and “be alert” across the Gospels and letters; the Gethsemane scene depends on the link with Mark 13 and with literal sleep."},{"lemma":"γραμματεύς","rendering":"scribe","verse":1,"reason":"Very frequent in the Gospels; versions divide between “scribes,” “teachers of the law” and “experts in the law,” and “scribe” may suggest a mere copyist to modern readers."},{"lemma":"ὑπηρέτης","rendering":"attendant","verse":54,"reason":"Recurs in the Gospels and Acts for temple and court personnel, rendered variously “officers,” “guards,” “servants” and “attendants,” and should be fixed so the same group is recognizable."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was two days before the Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to seize him by deceit and kill him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Not during the festival, or there may be an uproar among the people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was in Bethany, reclining at table in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came with an alabaster flask of perfumed oil—pure nard, very costly. She broke the flask and poured it over his head.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some who were there said indignantly to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why has this perfumed oil been wasted?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This perfumed oil could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they scolded her harshly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Leave her alone. Why are you making trouble for her? She has done a good thing for me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want you can do good to them, but you do not always have me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: She did what she could: she has anointed my body ahead of time for burial.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, wherever the good news is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went off to the chief priests to hand him over to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard it they were glad, and they promised to give him money. So he began looking for a good opportunity to hand him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, his disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where do you want us to go and make preparations for you to eat the Passover?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He sent two of his disciples and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and wherever he goes in, say to the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher says: Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He will show you a large upstairs room, furnished and ready. Make preparations for us there.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples set out and went into the city and found things just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over—one who is eating with me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They began to be distressed and to say to him one after another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Surely not I?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is one of the Twelve, the one who dips into the bowl with me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Son of Man goes as it is written about him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were eating, he took bread, said the blessing, broke it, and gave it to them, and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take it; this is my body.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, and they all drank from it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, I will never again drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Even if all fall away, I will not.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, today, this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you yourself will deny me three times.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he kept saying all the more forcefully,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they all said the same.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to a place named Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Sit here while I pray.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He took Peter, James, and John with him, and he began to be gripped by dread and anguish,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My soul is overwhelmed with grief, to the point of death. Stay here and keep awake.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Going on a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass him by.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Take this cup away from me. Yet not what I want, but what you want.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Simon, are you asleep? Did you not have the strength to keep awake for one hour?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Keep awake and pray, so that you do not come into testing. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down, and they did not know what to answer him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came the third time and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Get up, let us go. Look, the one handing me over has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once, while he was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the one handing him over had given them a signal, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The one I kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As soon as he arrived, he went up to him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and kissed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they laid hands on him and seized him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But one of those standing by drew his sword, struck the high priest’s slave, and cut off his ear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus responded and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if against a bandit?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Day after day I was with you in the temple, teaching, and you did not seize me. But this is so that the Scriptures may be fulfilled.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they all left him and fled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A certain young man was following him, wearing nothing but a linen cloth. They seized him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders, and the scribes came together.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the high priest’s courtyard, and he was sitting with the attendants and warming himself at the fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus in order to put him to death, but they were finding none.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For many were giving false testimony against him, and their testimonies did not agree.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some stood up and gave false testimony against him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We heard him say, ‘I will tear down this sanctuary made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet even on this point their testimony did not agree.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the high priest stood up in their midst and questioned Jesus:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have you no answer at all? What is it that these men are testifying against you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he stayed silent and gave no answer at all. Again the high priest questioned him and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am; and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The high priest tore his clothes and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What further need do we have of witnesses?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they all condemned him as deserving death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some began to spit on him, to cover his face and strike him with their fists, and to say to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Prophesy!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the attendants received him with slaps.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s slave girls came,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked straight at him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You too were with the Nazarene, Jesus.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he denied it, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I neither know nor understand what you are talking about.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went outside into the forecourt, and a rooster crowed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The slave girl saw him and began again to say to those standing by,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is one of them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But again he denied it. A little later those standing by again said to Peter,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You really are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech is like theirs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he began to call down curses and to swear an oath:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I do not know this man you are talking about.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once a rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered what Jesus had said to him:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he broke down and wept.

notes.note: The Greek word covers the range of ritually defiling scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which is broader than modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease) and may not include it. Elsewhere this translation says “skin disease”; here the traditional word is kept because it works as a byname identifying which Simon is meant. Since he is hosting a dinner, he was presumably no longer afflicted, though the text does not say.

The adjective describing the nard is rare and its meaning is uncertain. Most take it as “genuine” or “pure,” that is, unadulterated; others have suggested it names a variety of the plant or its source. Nard was an aromatic oil imported from the East, which explains its price.

notes.traditional: three hundred pence; three hundred denarii
notes.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a laborer. Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year’s wages.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same word for what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate and what Pilate then does. “Betray” names the treachery the context supplies, and some scholars defend it as a legitimate contextual sense; “hand over” lets the reader see the repeated word, as in verses 11, 18, 21, 41, 42 and 44.

The older rendering “be offended” now suggests hurt feelings. The verb pictures being tripped up so as to fall from loyalty, and here it refers to the disciples’ desertion that night; most modern versions also say “fall away.” The quotation that follows is from Zechariah 13:7.

Abba is the Aramaic word for “father,” used in addressing one’s own father by children and adults alike. Mark preserves the Aramaic and adds the Greek equivalent. The once-popular claim that it is baby talk equivalent to “Daddy” is no longer widely held.

Most versions have “temptation” here; some have “the time of trial.” In the usage of the period the word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will remain faithful, which is what the disciples are about to face. English “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin. Lexicons recognize both senses, and the two overlap here.

notes.phrase: Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough!
notes.traditional: Sleep on now, and take your rest: it is enough
notes.note: The first sentence can be read as a question, as a command (“Sleep on now and rest”), or as a reproachful exclamation. The single Greek word rendered “Enough!” is among the most debated in Mark: its usual meanings were “he has received in full” or “it is distant,” and proposals include “It is settled” and “He has been paid,” referring to Judas. “Enough” is the most common rendering but is uncertain.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. Some modern versions also say “slave.” The same applies to the “slave girls” of verses 66 and 69, where the Greek word means a female slave and is traditionally rendered “maid” or “servant girl.”

The Greek word denotes an armed, violent plunderer such as a highwayman, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some versions render it “rebel” here; that reading is possible but not certain. Most modern versions have “robber.”

Greek has two words usually both rendered “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts (as in verse 49) and this one for the building in which God was held to dwell. “Sanctuary” keeps them distinct. Most versions use “temple” for both, and scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers observe the distinction.

The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one,” the king Israel expected. Here it is a title under examination, not a name, so “Messiah” is used; several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. “Christ” is kept where the word functions as part of Jesus’ name.

“The Power,” like “the Blessed One” in the high priest’s question, is a reverent way of referring to God without naming him. Jesus’ reply combines Psalm 110:1, where the king sits at God’s right hand, with Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven.

These words are missing from several important early manuscripts, and some critical editions bracket them. They may have been added to prepare for the “second time” of verse 72, or removed to match the other Gospels, which mention only one crowing. The Greek text followed here includes them.

notes.phrase: and your speech is like theirs
notes.note: These words are absent from the earliest manuscripts and from most modern translations, though they stand in the majority of later manuscripts and in the King James Version. Many scholars think they were added under the influence of Matthew 26:73. The Greek text followed here includes them.

The verb means to place someone under a curse, and no object is expressed. Most understand that Peter invoked a curse on himself if he was lying; some scholars think he cursed Jesus. The traditional “curse and swear” can wrongly suggest profanity, whereas the Greek describes a solemn curse and a sworn denial.

notes.traditional: when he thought thereon, he wept
notes.note: The Greek participle before “wept” is obscure. Proposals include “he broke down,” “he began to,” “when he thought about it,” “he rushed outside,” and “covering his head.” None has won general agreement.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between “servant” and “slave,” which changes how readers picture households, parables and Paul’s self-descriptions.
Versions vary between “council” and the loanword “Sanhedrin” across the Gospels and Acts, and the choice should be uniform.
Rendered variously “watch,” “keep watch,” “stay awake” and “be alert” across the Gospels and letters; the Gethsemane scene depends on the link with Mark 13 and with literal sleep.
Very frequent in the Gospels; versions divide between “scribes,” “teachers of the law” and “experts in the law,” and “scribe” may suggest a mere copyist to modern readers.
Recurs in the Gospels and Acts for temple and court personnel, rendered variously “officers,” “guards,” “servants” and “attendants,” and should be fixed so the same group is recognizable.
